  One night, following a thin thread of woodsmoke, Remy found himself at the edge of a farmhouse. A lantern hung from the porch, swaying
  gently, casting amber light across the snow. Beneath it sat a bowl of scraps, steaming in the cold.

  He crept closer, belly low, every muscle taut. The bowl was almost within reach when a voice spoke from the dark.

  "Easy, friend."

  An old woman sat in a rocking chair, wrapped in wool, so still he had mistaken her for part of the porch. Remy froze, ready to bolt.

  "I put it out for you," she said softly. "Third winter now. You've got a limp in your left hind leg, I've noticed. Figured you could use
  the help."

  Remy stared. He had always believed the world was divided cleanly: hunters and hunted, and nothing in between. Yet here was a human who
  watched him without a gun, without a trap, only a lantern and a bowl.

  Slowly, warily, he ate. The warmth spread through him, chasing out the ache in his bones. The woman didn't move, didn't speak again, only
  rocked and hummed a tune he did not know.

  When he finished, he lingered a moment at the edge of the light. Then he turned and slipped into the trees.

  But he returned the next night, and the next. By spring, his leg had healed, and the woods had filled with food again. Still, on cold
  evenings, he would sit at the edge of the field and watch the lantern glow, remembering that kindness could be found in the strangest
  places.
